Mast Cells in Connective Tissue Mast cells are oval or irregularly shaped cells in connective tissue, measuring between 7 and 20 μm in diameter. They are filled with basophilic secretory granules that can obscure the central nucleus . Mast cell granules are electron dense , vary in size from 0.3 to 2.0 μm , and contain high levels of acidic radicals in their sulfated glycosaminoglycans ( GAGs ). Mast cell granules exhibit metachromasia , meaning they change the color of some basic dyes (like toluidine blue) from blue to purple or red. This staining feature is similar to basophils but mast cells are agranulocytes. It is common among very acidic substances like GAGs such as heparin. Due to the nature of their granules, mast cells may be difficult to identify in slides prepared with common fixatives .

Protein hormones are released by exocytosis , while lipophilic steroids diffuse through the cell membrane and are taken up by binding proteins outside the cell. Modes of Hormone Action in Endocrine System Hormones are distributed by the circulation system to act on distant target cells that possess specific receptors. Some endocrine cells produce hormones that act on nearby target cells , involving either paracrine or juxtacrine secretion. Paracrine secretion involves hormone dispersal in interstitial fluid or short blood vessel loops, like gastrin affecting fundic glands . In juxtacrine secretion , signaling molecules remain on the cell’s surface or adjacent matrix, affecting target cells upon direct contact , crucial in embryonic and regenerative tissues . Autocrine secretion occurs when cells produce molecules that act on themselves or similar cells , as seen with insulin-like growth factor (IGF) . Endocrine glands can be target organs for other hormones , creating a feedback mechanism to regulate hormone secretion and maintain stable blood hormone levels.

Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) and Antigen Presentation MHC Protein Complexes MHC proteins are specialized integral membrane protein complexes involved in antigen presentation. They are part of the major histocompatibility complex, crucial for immune responses. MHC includes two main types : MHC class I and MHC class II .

MHC Class II Protein Synthesis and Function Binding with Ingested Proteins MHC class II proteins bind to fragments of proteins ingested by the cell. These can include proteins from dead, infected, or abnormal cells , as well as atypical proteins . Presentation of Antigens and Activation of T Lymphocytes On the cell surface of APCs, MHC class II complexes display these peptide fragments . These displayed peptides signal especially ( CD4+ ) T lymphocytes , activating their immune responses against the sources of these antigens .

B Lymphocytes and B-Cell Receptors (BCRs) Antigen Binding and Processing BCRs can bind to antigens that are free in solution , part of infectious agents , or bound to antibodies . After binding, the antigen-BCR complexes undergo endocyto sis . Antigens are degraded in endosomes*, and peptides are presented on MHC class II molecules of the B cell.
Antigen Processing in Lymph Nodes Antigens not yet phagocytosed, are internalized by APCs in the lymph nodes. These antigens are then presented on MHC class II molecules .

T Cell and Antibody Circulation Specific T helper (Th) cells, cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs), and regulatory T (Tregs) cells recirculate through the e fferent lymph . Along with anti bodies , these cells spread immune defenses against microorganisms throughout the body .

Characteristics and Function of T Cells Longevity and Proportion in Blood T cells are long-lived lymphocytes. They constitute about 75% of circulating lymphocytes . Antigen Recognition T recognize antigenic epitopes through T-cell receptors (TCRs) on their surface. TCRs typically consist of 2 glycoproteins, known as the α and β chains . Each chain has varia ble regions , produced in a manner similar to those in immunoglobulins. MHC Restriction TCRs recognize antigenic peptides only when presented as part of MHC molecules . This interaction involves both the MHC molecule and the peptide it presents. Due to this specific recognition pattern, T lymphocytes are described as MHC restric ted .

Cytotoxic T Lymphocytes (CTLs) Role in Immune Response Function as Killer T Cells : CTLs attach to cells presenting the antigens (such as virus-infected cells) and initiate their destruction. Mechanism : They release perforins and granzymes to trigger apoptosis in target cells. This process is a key part of cell-mediated* immunity , similar in mechanism to NK cells ' actions in innate immunity.

Subpopulations of T Lymphocytes Regulatory T Cells (Tregs or Suppressor T Cells) Characteristics : Identified as CD4+CD25+ and express the Foxp3 transcription factor . Function : Inhibit specific immune responses. Allow immune tolerance by maintaining unresponsiveness to self-antigens. Suppress excessive immune responses . Role in Tolerance : Produce peripheral tolerance , supplementing the central tolerance that develops in the thymus.

Anaphylaxis: Sequence of Events Anaphylaxis starts with the first exposure to an allergen (e.g., bee venom), leading to the production of IgE antibodies by antibody-producing cells. These IgE antibodies bind avidly to receptors on mast cells . Upon a second exposure to the allergen, it reacts with the IgE on mast cells, triggering the rapid release of histamine , leukotrienes , chemokines , and heparin . This release leads to the sudden onset of the allergic reaction. Degranulation of mast cells also occurs due to the action of complement molecules involved in immunologic reactions.

Function : IgE facilitates allergic reactions by attach ing to allergens , the same substances that originally triggered the production of IgE .
